subject: physics
title: Newton's laws and free-body diagrams
key_idea: The resultant force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration, F = ma, and the acceleration is in the direction of the resultant force. A free-body diagram shows all the forces on one object, so the resultant can be found and Newton's laws applied.

blocks.text: Mass and weight are different quantities. This section covers what each means and how the newton is defined.

items.meaning: The property of an object that resists a change in its motion. A scalar, in kg.
The force on an object due to a gravitational field acting on its mass. A vector, in N.
The force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
The force per unit mass on a mass in a gravitational field.

blocks.label: Weight
where: g = gravitational field strength, equal to the acceleration of free fall (N/kg or m/s²)

blocks.label: Gravitational field strength
where: F = gravitational force on the mass (N)

items: Near the Earth's surface g is about 9.81 N/kg. The weight of an object equals its mass times the acceleration of free fall.
Mass stays the same everywhere. Weight changes with g, so it is different on the Moon.
Weight acts downwards, through the centre of gravity of the object.
Mass resists changes in motion. Weight is a force, W = mg.
1 N gives 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².

blocks.text: Newton's laws link force and motion. Each law applies to the forces acting on one object.

items.text: An object stays at rest, or moves at constant velocity, unless a resultant force acts on it.
The resultant force on an object is proportional to its rate of change of momentum, and acts in the same direction. For a constant mass this means the force is proportional to the acceleration.
If body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts an equal and opposite force on A.

items: If the resultant force is zero then a = 0. The object is at rest or moving at constant velocity, which is the first law.
Acceleration and resultant force are always in the same direction.
A greater resultant force gives a greater acceleration. A greater mass gives a smaller acceleration.
A resultant force changes the velocity of an object. It does not keep the object moving.
The second law in the form ΣF = ma applies when the mass is constant.

items.text: A 1200 kg car has a driving force of 3000 N and resistive forces of 1200 N. Find its acceleration.

diagram.alt: A practice calculation. Find the acceleration of an object from the driving force, the resistive force and the mass.
diagram.question: A trolley of mass {m} kg is pulled by a force of {F} N. A resistive force of {f} N opposes the motion. Calculate its acceleration.

items: Zero resultant force means constant velocity (first law).
ΣF = ma, with the acceleration in the direction of the resultant force.
Forces come in pairs between two bodies (third law).

blocks.text: Newton's third law describes a pair of forces. A pair always has the same set of matching properties.

items: The two forces are equal in magnitude.
They act in opposite directions.
They are the same type of force, for example both gravitational or both contact.
They act on two different bodies, never on the same one.
They act along the same line, at the same time.
The Earth pulls a book down with its weight. The book pulls the Earth up with an equal gravitational force. This is a pair.
A book on a table has its weight and the normal contact force acting on it. These are not a pair, because they act on the same object and are different types of force.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity. Sort each pair of forces into Newton's third law pairs and pairs that are not.
diagram.prompt: Is each pair of forces a Newton's third law pair?

items.text: The Earth pulls a book down. The book pulls the Earth up.
A swimmer pushes water backwards. The water pushes the swimmer forwards.
A rocket pushes gas downwards. The gas pushes the rocket upwards.
The weight of a book on a table and the table's contact force on it.
The weight of a skydiver and the drag on the skydiver.
The tension in a rope and the weight of the load it holds.

items: A third law pair acts on two different bodies, is equal and opposite and is the same type of force.
Two forces on the same body that balance are not a third law pair.

sections.heading: Types of force and free-body diagrams

blocks.text: A free-body diagram shows one object and every force acting on it. This section covers the forces and how to draw the diagram.

items.meaning: The pulling force along a stretched rope, string or cable.
The push of a surface on an object, at right angles to the surface.
The upward force on an object in a fluid, because pressure is greater at the bottom than the top.
The force between surfaces in contact that opposes relative motion or its tendency.
The constant velocity reached when the resistive force equals the driving force.

items.text: Draw the object alone, as a dot or a simple shape. A particle, or an extended rigid body.
Draw weight from the centre of gravity, straight down.
Add a force for every surface or rope touching the object. Normal forces are at right angles to the surface, and friction is along it.
Label each arrow with its name. Make lengths match the sizes.
Find the resultant by resolving along two perpendicular directions, then apply ΣF = ma.

items: Draw only forces on the object, not forces it exerts on others.
Do not include a separate force for the acceleration or for 'momentum'.
If the arrows balance, the object is at rest or at constant velocity.
A falling object with drag has weight down and drag up. At terminal velocity these are equal, so a = 0 and Newton's first law applies.
A free-body diagram shows every force on one object only.
Equal and opposite forces on one object give zero resultant and no acceleration.

checks.q: State Newton's third law, and explain why the weight of a book on a table and the table's contact force on it are not a third law pair.
checks.a: If body A exerts a force on body B, B exerts an equal and opposite force on A. The weight and contact force both act on the same body (the book), and they are different types of force.

checks.q: A 0.60 kg trolley accelerates at 2.5 m/s². Calculate the resultant force on it.
A skydiver falls at a constant velocity. Use Newton's laws to explain why.
checks.a: At constant velocity there is no acceleration, so by the first law the resultant force is zero. The upward drag equals her weight downwards, so the forces are balanced.

items: Apply the three laws of motion in appropriate situations.
F = ma is used for situations where the mass is constant.
Draw and interpret free-body force diagrams for a particle and for an extended rigid body.
Use the term terminal velocity: the velocity at which ΣF = 0 for an object moving through a resistive medium.
Know the properties of a pair of forces in an interaction between two bodies.
Recall F = ma and W = mg.
Describe motion in one and two dimensions under a constant force. Split the force into components, then apply ΣF = ma to each direction.
A constant force at right angles to the initial velocity gives a parabolic path, as for a projectile.
